findings.who: A Yonkers resident, or a self-employed filer in the MCTA region who pays the metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax (MCTMT) by estimated payments. They want part of the overpayment to cover 2026 Yonkers surcharge or MCTMT estimates.
findings.why_no: "Your 2026 New York tax" may read as New York State income tax only. The filer may enter zero, or a smaller amount, thinking the Yonkers or MCTMT estimate cannot be paid from the refund.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your New York State, New York City, Yonkers, and metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax estimated tax for 2026."
findings.fix: Ask: "How much of your New York overpayment should be applied to your 2026 estimated tax (New York State, New York City, Yonkers and MCTMT)?"

findings.who: A filer who directs part of the overpayment to NYS 529 accounts on Form IT-195 (line 78a).
findings.why_no: The help says "The rest is refunded to you." The filer may lower or misjudge the line 79 amount, thinking the remainder all comes back as a refund. The instructions say lines 78a through 79 together should equal line 77.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "The total of lines 78a through 79 should equal the amount on line 77."
findings.fix: Help: "The rest goes to any NYS 529 deposits you choose and is otherwise refunded to you."

findings.who: Spouses filing jointly who plan to make 2026 estimated payments, or where only the spouse expects 2026 self-employment or MCTMT liability.
findings.why_no: "Your 2026 New York tax" may read as the asking spouse's own tax only, so the couple may apply less than they intend.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your ... estimated tax for 2026."
findings.fix: On joint returns, say "your and your spouse's 2026 estimated tax".

findings.who: A New York resident who bought a $4,000 sofa in New Hampshire in 2024 while a New York resident, stored it out of state, and first brought it into New York for use in 2025; no New York sales tax was paid.
findings.why_no: The gate asks 'In 2025, did you ... buy'; they did not buy anything in 2025, so they answer no. The line also reaches a purchase made earlier and first used in New York this year.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'You owe sales or compensating use tax if you: ... purchased an item or service outside New York State that is subject to tax in New York State (and you were a resident of New York State at the time of purchase) with subsequent use in New York State.'

findings.who: A non-NYC New York resident who buys a $3,000 item in a New York locality with a lower combined rate than their home locality, or from an online seller that collects the lower rate, and uses it at home; they paid New York State and local sales tax, but less than their home locality's rate.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether they bought without paying New York sales tax; they did pay New York sales tax, just at a lower local rate, so they answer no. The help's 'Count a purchase taxed below New York City's rate' reads as an NYC-only rule and does not tell them to compare to their own locality's rate.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'You may also owe an additional local tax if you use property or services in another locality in New York State, other than the locality to which you paid tax. You owe use tax to the second locality if you were a resident of that locality at the time of the purchase, and its rate of tax is higher than the rate of tax originally paid.'

findings.who: A New Jersey income-tax resident who owns a Manhattan apartment (a permanent place of abode) and buys taxable goods online from a no-tax state, delivered to that apartment, for use there.
findings.why_no: They know they are not a New York income-tax resident and answer no to buying taxable goods in New York; the instructions make a person with a New York permanent place of abode a sales-tax resident even if not an income-tax resident.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'For sales and use tax purposes, a resident includes persons who have a permanent place of abode in the state. Accordingly, you may be a resident for sales tax purposes even though you may not be a resident for income tax purposes.'

findings.who: A sole proprietor who buys $5,000 of taxable equipment online for a business that is not registered for New York sales tax, and the seller charges no New York tax.
findings.why_no: The help says 'Leave out purchases of a business registered for sales tax'; the filer reads that as leaving out business purchases generally, or does not know whether the business is registered, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'You may not use this line to report: ... any sales and use tax on business purchases if the business is registered for sales and use tax purposes. You must report this tax on the business’s sales tax return.' The same page says the chart may not be used for purchases related to a business not registered for sales tax purposes.

findings.who: A commuter domiciled in Connecticut, New Jersey or Westchester who keeps a Manhattan apartment all year and spends 184 or more days (counting part days) in New York City.
findings.why_no: "Did you live in New York City ... for all of 2025?" asks where the filer lived. The help covers only time away from a city home. This filer's home is in the suburbs, so the truthful answer is no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "You maintain a permanent place of abode in New York State for substantially all of the tax year and spend 184 days or more in New York State"; p. 31: "substitute New York City or Yonkers in place of New York State"
findings.fix: Ask about the statutory test directly. First ask whether the filer (or spouse) kept a place to live in New York City for nearly all of 2025. If yes, ask how many days, counting any part of a day, they spent in the city. Treat a city resident as anyone domiciled in the city or meeting both parts of the test, then route on that result.

findings.who: A filer domiciled in New York City who spent all of 2025 on a temporary work assignment in Atlanta or abroad. They sublet or gave up the city apartment, plan to return, and visited the city more than 30 days, so the Group A exception does not apply.
findings.why_no: The help counts time away only "if your home stayed in the city". With no city apartment, the filer did not "live" in the city at all in 2025 and answers no. Their domicile is still the city.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "If you move to a new location but intend to stay there only for a limited amount of time (no matter how long), your domicile does not change." Also: "Your domicile is New York State. However ... you are not a resident if you meet all three of the conditions in either Group A or Group B"
findings.fix: Ask separately whether the filer's permanent home, the place they intend to return to, was in New York City all year, even if they lived elsewhere temporarily. Apply the Group A and Group B exceptions only after a yes.

findings.who: A filer who moved from Brooklyn to Florida in 2025 but kept the Brooklyn apartment, kept their job ties and family in the city, and expects to come back. The move does not meet the clear-and-convincing standard for a change of domicile.
findings.why_no: The filer reads "for all of 2025" by the calendar: they moved out in the spring, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "A change of domicile is clear and convincing only when your primary ties are clearly greater in the new location." Also: "Your New York domicile does not change until you can demonstrate that you have abandoned your New York domicile"
findings.fix: After a no, ask whether the filer moved away from the city in 2025. If so, ask whether they kept their city home and their main ties there. If they did, treat them as still domiciled in the city, or refer them for a domicile review.

findings.who: A graduate, law or medical student, or a full-time undergraduate's spouse, who is domiciled elsewhere and lives all year in university housing in Manhattan, spending more than 184 days in the city.
findings.why_no: The help says "A college dorm does not count as a home." The student reads it as covering every student residence and answers no. The exclusion applies only to full-time undergraduates in a baccalaureate program.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "a residence maintained by a full-time student enrolled at an institution of higher education in an undergraduate degree program leading to a baccalaureate degree and occupied by the student while attending the institution is not a permanent place of abode with respect to that student"
findings.fix: Change the help to: "Housing you occupied as a full-time undergraduate student working toward a bachelor's degree does not count as a place to live. Graduate students' university housing does count."

findings.who: A commuter who keeps a city apartment and counts only nights slept there (for example 150). Counting every workday they set foot in the city, they reach more than 184 days.
findings.why_no: Neither the gate help nor the State question help says that any part of a day counts as a day. The filer counts nights and decides they did not live in the city.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "*Any part of a day is a day for this purpose."
findings.fix: Ask for a day count with this help: "Count every day you were in New York City for any part of the day, including commuting days."

findings.who: A joint filer who moved into the city mid-2025 while their spouse lived in the city all year, or who lived in the city all year while the spouse lived elsewhere.
findings.why_no: The gate says "you", while the line's helper tests "you (and your spouse, on a joint return)". Spouses with different residency statuses may need different handling for the joint return, and the gate question does not ask about the spouse.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "A permanent place of abode usually includes a residence your spouse owns or leases." Also, Group B: "You, your spouse (unless legally separated) and minor children spent 90 days or less"
findings.fix: Ask the gate as "Did you and your spouse each ...", record each spouse's answer, and route mixed answers to the part-year or nonresident path.

findings.who: A member of the military, or a military spouse, whose legal residence is New York City but who is stationed or living elsewhere.
findings.why_no: The filer has not lived in the city for the year and answers no. Their residency is governed by special SCRA rules that the gate does not mention.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "Note: Special rules under the SCRA apply to members of the military and their spouses for determining residency."
findings.fix: Add a screening question: "Were you or your spouse in active military service, or a military spouse, in 2025?" Route a yes to the military residency rules.

findings.why_no: The gate asks about 'New York income tax,' and the help lists only 'State, City or commuter (MCTMT)' tax; it never names Yonkers, so the filer reads the list as complete and answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 22, Line 75: 'your 2025 estimated tax payments for New York State, New York City, Yonkers, and metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax'
findings.fix: Add 'Yonkers' to the gate and help, or ask broadly whether the filer made any 2025 New York State, New York City, Yonkers, or MCTMT estimated tax payment.

findings.who: A beneficiary of an estate or trust that paid 2025 New York estimated tax and allocated the beneficiary's share on the required notification, but did not distribute cash to the beneficiary.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'have estimated tax passed to you'; the filer reads 'passed' as money distributed to them, not as an allocation of estimated tax paid on their behalf, and the help does not mention estate or trust allocations.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 22, Line 75: 'your portion of any payment of estimated taxes allocated to you by the estate or trust' and 'submit a copy of the notification issued by the estate or trust'

findings.who: Married filing jointly; the spouse, not the filer, bought taxable personal goods online delivered to their New York home and no New York sales tax was collected. They maintained a New York abode for only part of 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether 'you' bought the goods; the filer truthfully answers no for themselves and the wording never says 'you or your spouse'.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18, Line 59: Sales or use tax: 'Report your sales or use tax liability on this line' and 'You owe sales or compensating use tax if you: • purchased an item or service subject to tax...'
findings.fix: Ask 'Did you or your spouse buy...' and include either spouse's untaxed purchases in the line 59 and abode-proration computation.

findings.who: A New York resident bought a taxable item out of state in 2023, stored it, and first brought it into New York in 2025; the filer maintained a New York abode for only part of 2025.
findings.why_no: In the annual return context the filer reads 'Bought' as asking about purchases made in 2025, so they say no because the purchase was years earlier.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18, Line 59: Sales or use tax: 'purchased an item or service outside New York State ... with subsequent use in New York State.'
findings.fix: Ask whether in 2025 the filer first used or brought into New York any taxable item purchased without New York tax, regardless of the purchase year.

findings.who: A part-year New York abode holder who is not a New York income tax resident bought taxable goods online delivered to the New York apartment and paid no New York tax; they think nonresidents do not owe New York use tax.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'taxable in New York' without telling them that a permanent place of abode makes them a New York sales-tax resident, so they answer no because they are not a New York resident for income tax.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18, Line 59: Sales or use tax: 'For sales and use tax purposes, a resident includes persons who have a permanent place of abode in the state. Accordingly, you may be a resident for sales tax purposes even though you may not be a resident for income tax purposes.'
findings.fix: State that a permanent place of abode makes the filer a New York sales-tax resident for these purchases; ask whether goods were delivered to or used at that New York home.

findings.who: A filer bought a taxable laptop online delivered to New York and paid no sales tax; they had no vehicle or vessel purchase. When asked 'Not every untaxed purchase was a vehicle or vessel taxed at the DMV,' they answer no.
findings.why_no: The double-negative helper is read as asking whether they had a vehicle or vessel; they say no, although the statement is true for their laptop purchase.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18, Line 59: Sales or use tax: 'You owe sales or compensating use tax if you: • purchased an item or service subject to tax that is delivered to you in New York State without payment of New York State and local tax to the seller...'
findings.fix: Replace the helper with 'Were all of your untaxed purchases vehicles or vessels taxed at the DMV?' (yes -> no; no -> yes) or ask directly whether there was any untaxed purchase other than a DMV-taxed vehicle or vessel.

findings.who: An individual bought personal goods online from a New York seller that collected no tax, and the individual also owns a business registered for New York sales tax. They read 'other than purchases of a business registered for sales tax' as excluding them because they have a registered business.
findings.why_no: The phrase 'purchases of a business registered for sales tax' is ambiguous; they take it to exclude personal purchases or purchases from a registered seller.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18, Line 59: Sales or use tax: 'You may not use this line to report: • any sales and use tax on business purchases if the business is registered for sales and use tax purposes.'
findings.fix: Say 'other than business purchases made by a business registered for New York sales tax' and add that personal purchases by an owner remain reportable.

findings.who: A filer bought taxable goods from a television shopping channel (or on an Indian reservation other than Oneida) and paid no New York tax; they read the gate's examples 'online, by catalog, or out of state' as the complete list.
findings.why_no: The examples omit categories the instructions expressly name, so the filer takes the list as exhaustive and answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18, Line 59: Sales or use tax: 'An unpaid sales or use tax liability commonly occurs if you made purchases through the Internet, by catalog, from television shopping channels, or on an Indian reservation (except for purchases subject to Oneida Nation taxes)...'
findings.fix: Add television shopping and Indian reservation purchases to the examples, or drop the examples and use the broad 'purchased an item or service subject to tax' wording.

findings.who: A filer (or joint filer and spouse) with no New York estimated tax payments on line 75, whose only prepayment is wage withholding that is less than the required annual payment—for example, a wage earner with a large bonus or investment income, or a self-employed filer with no withholding.
findings.why_no: The computed gate requires 'Estimated tax payments (line 75) more than zero'; with line 75 at zero it is false, so the tool never asks whether any estimated installment was skipped and treats the late/short-installment line as no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 81: 'You may owe an estimated tax penalty if you did not have enough tax withheld from your wages or did not make enough estimated tax payments on other income you earned during the year.'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate: ask the late/short-installment question whenever total 2025 prepayments (withholding plus estimated payments, including payments made on the filer's behalf) may be below the required annual payment, or whenever line 80 is $300 or more and more than 10% of the tax; treat zero estimated payments as skipped installments when an installment was required.

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly where only the spouse's employer provided dependent care benefits (for example, through the spouse's dependent care FSA, W-2 box 10), or only the spouse paid the daycare provider from the spouse's own account.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed from the f2441 helpers 'Did you pay for the care of a qualifying person so you could work or look for work?' and 'Did you receive dependent care benefits?', which say only 'you'. The filer truthfully answers no for themselves. The displayed text says 'you (or your spouse)', but the inputs that drive the condition do not.
findings.irs_text: ny_it216i p. 1: 'The care was provided so you (and your spouse, if you were married) could work or look for work.'; 'Caution: Taxpayers who receive dependent care benefits from their employer must complete Worksheet 1 – Dependent care benefits.'
findings.fix: Word both f2441 helpers as 'Did you or your spouse pay for…' and 'Did you or your spouse receive dependent care benefits (for example, Form W-2 box 10 or a dependent care FSA)?', or ask a per-return gate that names the spouse.

findings.who: An employee whose employer paid the care provider directly, ran an on-site daycare, or reimbursed care through a dependent care FSA funded by salary reduction. The employee never handed over money for care and never thinks of having 'received' a benefit.
findings.why_no: 'Did you pay for the care' reads as no because the FSA or employer paid. 'Did you receive dependent care benefits' reads as no because no cash was received, and nothing points the filer to Form W-2 box 10.
findings.irs_text: ny_it216i p. 1: 'Caution: Taxpayers who receive dependent care benefits from their employer must complete Worksheet 1 – Dependent care benefits.'
findings.fix: Add help: 'Include care paid through a dependent care FSA or flexible spending plan, care your employer paid for or provided on site, and any amount in Form W-2 box 10.'

findings.who: A filer who paid for care of a disabled spouse or a disabled adult dependent (for example, a parent living with them) so they could work. Or a filer whose child turned 13 during 2025, with care paid for the months before the birthday.
findings.why_no: 'Care of a qualifying person' and 'child and dependent care' read as childcare for young children. The filer does not see adult care or the part-year care of a child who turned 13 as covered.
findings.irs_text: ny_it216i p. 1: 'Your spouse who is disabled and not able to care for themself and lived with you for more than half the year.'; 'If the child turned 13 during the year, the child is a qualifying person for the part of the year they were under age 13.'
findings.fix: Add help: 'A qualifying person includes a child under 13 (for the part of the year under 13), a disabled spouse, or a disabled person who lived with you more than half the year and whom you claim or could claim as a dependent.'

findings.who: A working parent who paid for summer day camp, a before- or after-school program, preschool or nursery school, or a grandparent or other relative (not a dependent) who babysat while the parents worked.
findings.why_no: These payments are not perceived as 'care expenses'. Camp and after-school programs read as activities, preschool reads as education, and paying a relative reads as informal family help.
findings.irs_text: ny_it216i p. 1: 'The person who provided the care was not your spouse, the parent of your qualifying child under age 13, or a person whom you can claim as a dependent. If your child (including stepchild or foster child) provided the care, they must have been age 19 or older by December 31.'
findings.fix: Add help listing examples: 'daycare, preschool, before/after-school programs, day camp (not overnight camp), and paid babysitters, including relatives who are not your dependents.'

findings.who: A filer who in 2025 paid a provider's bill for care given in late 2024, or who prepaid in 2024 for care provided in 2025.
findings.why_no: A filer who reads the helper as asking about 2025 care paid in 2025 answers no when the payment and the care fall in different years.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 19, Line 64: 'Would you qualify to claim the federal child and dependent care credit for 2025 (whether or not you actually claimed it)?'
findings.fix: Add help: 'Answer yes if you paid in 2025 for care given in an earlier year, or if care given in 2025 was paid earlier.'

findings.who: A retired employee of the District of Columbia or of a U.S. territory or possession (for example, Puerto Rico) who receives a government pension included in federal AGI on IT-201 line 9 or 10.
findings.why_no: The question asks only about 'the federal government, the military, or a New York State or local government job'; a DC or territorial government pension is none of those, and the help does not mention them.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9: 'The United States, its territories, possessions (or political subdivisions thereof), ... or the District of Columbia.'
findings.fix: Ask about a 'federal, military, New York State or local, District of Columbia, or U.S. territory/possession government job' and repeat the list in the help.

findings.who: A retiree whose pension is from the MTA Police 20-Year Retirement Program, MABSTOA, or the Long Island Rail Road and is included in federal AGI on line 9 or 10.
findings.why_no: The question says 'New York State or local government job'; a public authority such as the MTA, MABSTOA, or LIRR is not the state or a local government, and the help names no public authority.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9: 'Certain public authorities, including: • Metropolitan Transit Authority (MTA) Police 20-Year Retirement Program; • Manhattan and Bronx Surface Transit Operating Authority (MABSTOA); and • Long Island Railroad Company.'
findings.fix: Name the MTA Police 20-Year Retirement Program, MABSTOA, and LIRR in the question or help, or ask about a 'New York public authority' pension.

findings.who: A retired SUNY/CUNY or State Education Department employee in the Optional Retirement Program whose pension is an annuity paid by TIAA or another insurer and is included in federal AGI on line 9 or 10.
findings.why_no: The question asks about a 'New York State ... government job,' but the filer sees a TIAA/insurer annuity and the help does not mention the Optional Retirement Program or TIAA; they read it as a private annuity, not a government pension.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9: 'New York State, including State and City University of New York and New York State Education Department employees who belong to the Optional Retirement Program.'
findings.fix: Mention the Optional Retirement Program and the TIAA example in the help, or ask about 'an ORP annuity paid by TIAA or another insurer.'

findings.who: A joint filer who personally has no IRA, pension, or annuity income, but whose spouse has taxable government pension income on line 9 or 10 (or a disability pension in federal wages on line 1h).
findings.why_no: The gate helper asks 'Is there taxable IRA, pension or annuity income on line 9 or 10?' without 'you or your spouse'; the filer answers for themselves and says no, so the government pension question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9: 'Did you receive a pension or other distribution ... that was included in your federal adjusted gross income?'
findings.fix: Add 'you or your spouse' to both gate helpers: line 9/10 income and line 1h disability pension.

findings.who: A retired New York City employee, teacher, police officer, or NYS and Local Retirement System member receives a local/state pension included in federal AGI. They answer No to the initial question because they do not think their city, school, police, or retirement-system pension is the kind of 'New York State or local government pension plan' meant; the gated question then names only MTA/MABSTOA/LIRR/SUNY/CUNY/SED, so they truthfully answer No.
findings.why_no: The gated question's list is read as complete; their local or state retirement-system plan is not one of the named plans.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: 'New York State... – Local governments within the state.'
findings.fix: Broaden the gated question to any New York State or local government pension plan, including NYCERS, NYSTRS, NYS and Local Retirement System, police/fire, and other state/local plans.

findings.who: A retired MTA Police officer receives a pension from the MTA Police 20-Year Retirement Program included in federal AGI. They answer No to the initial question if they think MTA Police is not the MTA transit system; the gated question says 'MTA' but not 'MTA Police 20-Year Retirement Program', so they answer No.
findings.why_no: The gated question names 'MTA' but omits the MTA Police 20-Year Retirement Program; the filer reads the list as not covering MTA Police.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: 'Metropolitan Transit Authority (MTA) Police 20-Year Retirement Program'
findings.fix: Name the MTA Police 20-Year Retirement Program explicitly and use 'including but not limited to' for public authorities.

findings.who: A divorced filer receives part of an ex-spouse's NYS and Local Retirement System or federal pension under a QDRO; the distribution is included in federal AGI. They answer No to the initial question because they were not the government employee, and No to the gated question because the plan is not MTA/MABSTOA/LIRR/SUNY/CUNY/SED.
findings.why_no: The initial question reads as employee-only; the gated question's list does not mention a nonemployee spouse or QDRO.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: 'Nonemployee spouses You may include distributions you received from a New York State or local pension plan or from a federal government pension plan as a nonemployee spouse in accordance with a court-issued qualified domestic relations order (QDRO)...'
findings.fix: Ask whether you, your spouse, or a nonemployee spouse under a QDRO received the distribution, and broaden the gated question beyond the named plans.

findings.who: A filer receives a survivor pension as the beneficiary of a deceased parent who worked for a local government or federal agency (not MTA/SUNY); included in federal AGI. They answer No to the initial question because they were not the employee, and No to the gated question because the named plans do not fit.
findings.why_no: They read the question as employee-only; the gated question names plans, not beneficiaries.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: 'enter the amount of any pension you received ... as an officer, employee, or beneficiary of an officer or employee of any of the following'
findings.fix: Add 'or as a beneficiary' to the question and do not limit the follow-up to the named plans.

findings.who: A taxpayer files jointly; only the spouse receives a pension from the MTA included in federal AGI. The taxpayer answers No to 'Did you receive' because it was the spouse's, and then answers No to 'Was any of it from the MTA' because the question says 'you' rather than 'you or your spouse'.
findings.why_no: The gate and gated question say 'you'; the taxpayer reads them as asking only about the taxpayer personally.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: enter the amount of any pension you received ... as an officer, employee, or beneficiary ... Metropolitan Transit Authority (MTA) Police 20-Year Retirement Program...
findings.fix: Use 'you or your spouse' in both the government pension question and the gated MTA/SUNY question.

findings.who: A retired MTA Police officer receives a line-of-duty disability pension reported in W-2 wages. The filer does not describe it as a 'disability pension in wages' (it is called disability retirement or injury pay), so the gate helper is false and the gated question is never asked.
findings.why_no: The helper says 'disability pension in wages'; the filer thinks their line-of-duty disability retirement is not a pension.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: 'pension you received—or any distributions made to you from a pension plan ... as an officer, employee, or beneficiary ... MTA Police 20-Year Retirement Program'
findings.fix: Ask a broad question about any W-2 wage amount that is a disability retirement or line-of-duty pension from a government employer, with examples.

findings.who: A military retiree receives military retirement pay included in federal AGI. They answer No to the initial question because it says 'federal government pension plan' and does not mention military retirement; the gated question lists only NY public plans, so they answer No.
findings.why_no: The initial question omits military retirement; the gated question's list is read as complete.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: '... any agency or instrumentality of the United States (including the military) ...'
findings.fix: Mention military retirement and federal plans in the gated question; ask 'federal, military, or other U.S. government pension'.

findings.fix: Broaden the gate and the question to cover both account owners and beneficiaries: ask whether the filer or spouse owned a New York 529 account or received a beneficiary withdrawal in 2025, and compute line 30 from contributions plus any qualified distribution included in federal AGI.

findings.who: A married filer filing a joint IT-201 whose spouse received a New York inflation refund check in fall 2025 and included it in the joint federal AGI as a state tax refund or other income; the filer personally did not receive or include it.
findings.why_no: The gate says "A state tax refund or other income on federal Schedule 1" and does not say "you or your spouse." The filer reads "you" as self alone and answers no, so the tool never asks the inflation-check question.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 25: "If you received an inflation refund check from the Tax Department and included the check amount in the calculation of federal adjusted gross income reported on line 19, then enter that amount on line 25."
findings.fix: Word the gate "you or your spouse" and compute it from the joint Schedule 1 lines; if either spouse received and included the check, the gate must be true.

findings.who: A self-employed filer who deposited the New York inflation refund check into a business account and reported it as gross business income on Schedule C, so it flows to federal Schedule 1 line 3 and into federal AGI, with no state tax refund on line 1 and no amount on line 9.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only for a state tax refund or other income on Schedule 1 line 1 or line 9. The filer truthfully says no because the check was business income, not a state refund or Schedule 1 "other income."
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 25: "If you received an inflation refund check from the Tax Department and included the check amount in the calculation of federal adjusted gross income reported on line 19, then enter that amount on line 25."
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to ask whether the filer or spouse received a New York inflation refund check and included it in federal AGI, regardless of the federal line or schedule used; do not restrict it to Schedule 1 line 1 or line 9.

findings.who: A filer who included the New York inflation refund check as other income on federal Schedule 1 but also has an equal negative other-income or loss amount, so Schedule 1 line 9 nets to exactly zero.
findings.why_no: The computed gate requires line 9 to be not zero. The check amount is included in federal AGI, but the net line 9 is zero, so the tool computes the gate false and never asks about the check.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 25: "If you received an inflation refund check from the Tax Department and included the check amount in the calculation of federal adjusted gross income reported on line 19, then enter that amount on line 25."
findings.fix: Gate on the presence or gross amount of the inflation check itself, or on any Schedule 1 line containing it, not on whether the net line 9 is nonzero.

findings.who: A filer whose gate is true because of an unrelated state tax refund on Schedule 1 line 1, and who also received the New York inflation refund check but included it in federal AGI as business income on Schedule C/Schedule 1 line 3.
findings.why_no: The gated question asks whether the check was included "as a state tax refund or as other income." The filer reads that list as exhaustive and answers no because it was included as business income, not in either named category.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 25: "If you received an inflation refund check from the Tax Department and included the check amount in the calculation of federal adjusted gross income reported on line 19, then enter that amount on line 25."
findings.fix: Remove the "as a state tax refund or as other income" limitation and ask whether the filer included the New York inflation refund check in federal income or federal AGI in any manner.

findings.who: A filer whose preparer reported the New York inflation refund check as additional wages on Form 1040 line 1a or as interest on line 2b, so the check is in federal AGI but there is no Schedule 1 line 1 or line 9 amount.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about federal Schedule 1. The filer truthfully says no to having a Schedule 1 state refund or other income, even though the check is included in federal AGI.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 25: "If you received an inflation refund check from the Tax Department and included the check amount in the calculation of federal adjusted gross income reported on line 19, then enter that amount on line 25."
findings.fix: Ask directly about receipt and inclusion in federal AGI rather than using Schedule 1 line 1 or line 9 as a proxy for inclusion.

findings.who: A New York City or Yonkers resident, or a self-employed filer in the MCTD who owes MCTMT. They want this year's overpayment credited to their 2026 city, Yonkers, or MCTMT estimated tax.
findings.why_no: The question says "your 2026 New York tax" and the help says "New York estimated tax". A filer may read this as New York State income tax only, so they answer no and plan to pay the city, Yonkers, or MCTMT estimate separately.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your New York State, New York City, Yonkers, and metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax estimated tax for 2026."
findings.fix: Ask: "Do you or your spouse want any of your New York overpayment applied to your 2026 New York State, New York City, Yonkers, or MCTMT estimated tax instead of refunded?"

findings.who: Spouses filing a joint return. One spouse makes the 2026 estimated payments, and the other spouse answers the tool's questions.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether "you" want "your" refund kept. The answering spouse does not plan to pay estimated tax and answers no for the couple.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your ... estimated tax for 2026."
findings.fix: Say "you or your spouse" on joint returns.

findings.who: A filer with an overpayment on line 77 who plans to direct part of it to NYS 529 accounts on line 78a. They see the rest as a credit, not a "refund".
findings.why_no: The question uses the word "refund", but line 78 is the refund that remains after line 79 is taken out. A filer who expects no check may think they have no "refund" to keep.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 78: "Subtract the amount on line 79 (estimated tax) from line 77. This is the amount available for refund."
findings.fix: Use "overpayment (line 77)" in place of "refund". Show the line 77 amount in the question.

findings.who: A filer with an overpayment on line 77 who is first asked how much of it to apply to 2026 estimated tax and enters the whole overpayment, planning to direct part of it to a 529 account later. Line 78 then computes as zero.
findings.why_no: No answer from the filer is involved; the gate is computed. If the tool asks for the line 79 amount before the 529 question, a full line 79 entry makes line 78 zero, and the 529 question is never shown. The filer never sees that line 78a and line 79 compete for the same line 77 overpayment.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your ... estimated tax for 2026. The total of lines 78a through 79 should equal the amount on line 77."; Line 78: "Subtract the amount on line 79 (estimated tax) from line 77."
findings.fix: Ask about the 529 deposit (or base the gate on line 77 > $0) before asking for the line 79 amount, or say in the line 79 question that any amount applied to estimated tax cannot also go to a 529 account or be refunded.

findings.who: A filer owns an out-of-state municipal bond bought at a premium; the bond pays tax-exempt interest in 2025, but bond-premium amortization leaves federal Form 1040 line 2a at zero.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only 'Was tax-exempt interest received in 2025?' and the filer answers No because line 2a is zero after premium; the parenthetical about premium is not in the question itself.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 7, Line 20: 'If Yes, enter any such interest income that you received or that was credited to you during 2025...' and 'For purposes of this addition, bond premium amortization is not allowed as a direct offset to interest income.'
findings.fix: Ask whether the filer or spouse received or had credited any interest from state or local bonds or tax-exempt bond funds before bond-premium amortization, and gate on 1099-INT box 8 or 1099-DIV box 13 as well as line 2a.

findings.who: A filer sold an out-of-state municipal bond between interest dates and received accrued interest from the buyer as part of the sale price, with no coupon payment and no amount on federal line 2a.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether tax-exempt interest was 'received'; the filer thinks of interest as coupon payments and answers No, not treating accrued interest embedded in the sale proceeds as tax-exempt interest.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 7, Line 20: 'If you sold a bond between interest dates, include the amount of interest you received during the year plus the accrued interest amount...'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to cover accrued interest on bonds bought or sold between interest dates, including accrued interest paid by the buyer, and ask about it explicitly.

findings.who: A filer whose only tax-exempt income is exempt-interest dividends from a national tax-free bond fund or a tax-exempt money market fund; the filer received dividends, not 'interest,' and may leave federal line 2a at zero.
findings.why_no: The gate question says 'Was tax-exempt interest received?' and does not mention exempt-interest dividends or fund dividends, so the filer answers No.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 7, Line 20: 'This includes interest income on: ... interest and dividend income from tax-exempt bond mutual funds, and tax-exempt money market funds that invest in obligations of states other than New York.'
findings.fix: Ask 'tax-exempt interest or exempt-interest dividends, including from tax-exempt bond mutual funds or money market funds' and gate on 1099-DIV box 13 or line 2a.

findings.who: On a joint return, only the spouse received out-of-state municipal bond interest that is not reflected on the joint federal line 2a, such as accrued interest on a sale or gross interest eliminated by bond premium; the primary filer answers No because the helper asks whether 'you' received it.
findings.why_no: The helper uses 'you' and does not say 'you or your spouse,' so the primary filer answers No for himself or herself.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 7, Line 20: 'If Yes, enter any such interest income that you received or that was credited to you during 2025...'
findings.fix: Ask 'Did you or your spouse receive or have credited...' and compute the gate from the joint federal line 2a plus either spouse's 1099s.

findings.who: A partner or S corporation shareholder is allocated out-of-state municipal bond interest on a K-1 but receives no cash distribution; the entity reports a New York addition for line 20, but the filer answers No because the interest was allocated, not paid.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether tax-exempt interest was 'received' in 2025; an allocation on a K-1 is not a receipt to the filer.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 7: 'Partners and S corporation shareholders ... EA-113 Interest income on state and local bonds and obligations 20.'
findings.fix: Include interest allocated to the filer on a Schedule K-1 from a partnership, S corporation, estate, or trust, even if no cash was distributed.

findings.who: A low-income tenant-stockholder in a cooperative housing corporation pays monthly maintenance of more than $450, which includes the co-op's real property taxes, and the unit's market value is $85,000 or less.
findings.why_no: They do not pay rent and do not own real estate in the ordinary sense; they own shares and pay maintenance, so both branches of the question read false.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 2, Step 4: 'A condominium, a cooperative, or a rental unit within a single dwelling is also a residence'; p. 2, line 15: 'Real property taxes paid also include any real estate taxes allowed ... as a deduction for tenant-stockholders in a cooperative housing corporation under IRC section 216.'
findings.fix: Ask about rent, co-op maintenance/tenant-stockholder status, or owning a home, condo, mobile home, or other real estate; state that the $450 rent cap does not apply to homeowners/co-op owners.

findings.who: A low-income filer owns a mobile home that is assessed for real property tax and pays the taxes, but rents the lot for more than $450 a month; the mobile home's market value is $85,000 or less.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether they pay rent of $450 or less or own real estate of $85,000 or less; they do not own land/real estate in the ordinary sense and their lot rent is over $450.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 2, Step 4: 'A trailer or mobile home that is used only for residential purposes is also a residence if the trailer or mobile home is assessed for real property tax purposes'; 'Mobile homeowners who pay the real property taxes should follow the instructions for homeowners.'
findings.fix: Ask about owning a house, condominium, cooperative shares, or an assessed mobile home/trailer, and about real property taxes paid, not just rent or real estate.

findings.who: A low-income renter pays $500 a month including heat; after subtracting the heat charge, adjusted rent is $440, and the filer is not a dependent.
findings.why_no: They compare the $500 paid to the $450 limit and answer no, because they do not have a separate heat charge or do not treat the parenthetical as a computation.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 2, line 12: 'Adjusted rent is the rent paid after subtracting any charges for heat, gas, electricity, furnishings, and board.'
findings.fix: Ask for adjusted rent after subtracting those charges, with a 'don't know' path and an example.

findings.who: A low-income renter occupied one New York apartment for seven months at $400 a month and another for five months at $800 a month; the first residence meets the six-month and rent tests, but the annual average rent exceeds $450.
findings.why_no: They average all 2025 rent and answer no, even though the instructions apply the rent limit per rented property and the six-month test to the first residence.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 1: 'The average monthly rent you or your spouse ... paid was $450 or less'; p. 1 note: 'If the current average monthly rent paid for a rented property ... was more than $450, then no credit is allowed for any renters of that rented property'; p. 2, line 12: 'If you moved from one rented residence to another rented residence, calculate the adjusted rent for each residence.'
findings.fix: Ask on a per-residence basis whether any New York residence occupied six months or more had adjusted rent of $450 or less; do not use a blended annual average.

findings.who: A low-income renter shares an apartment; the total rent is $900 a month, but the filer's share is $450 or less and the filer paid only that share.
findings.why_no: They read 'pay rent averaging $450 a month or less' as the apartment's total rent, not the rent the filer actually paid after the roommate's share.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 2, line 11: 'Enter the total rent you or your spouse ... paid during 2025'; line 12: 'Adjusted rent is the rent paid after subtracting any charges...'
findings.fix: Ask for the rent paid by the filer/spouse, after reimbursements from roommates, not the household's total rent.

findings.who: A low-income homeowner's house has a current market value of $80,000 and a mortgage of $70,000; the filer thinks the bank owns the home or that 'worth' means net equity.
findings.why_no: They read 'own real estate worth $85,000 or less' as requiring outright ownership or using equity rather than current market value.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 1: 'The current market value of all real property you owned ... was $85,000 or less'; p. 1 note: 'If the current market value of a real property is more than $85,000...'
findings.fix: Ask about current market value, not equity or mortgage balance, and state that a mortgage does not mean the filer does not own the home.

findings.who: A general partner or member of an LLC taxed as a partnership, such as a Manhattan law-firm partner, with $200,000 of net earnings from self-employment reported on Schedule K-1 and no Schedule C. On a joint return, the spouse may be the partner.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed from Schedule C alone: more than one Schedule C, or Schedule C net profit over $50,000. With no Schedule C the count is zero, the gate is false, and the MCTMT question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "For purposes of the MCTMT, self-employed individuals include: • Sole proprietors • Partners in partnerships • Members of limited liability companies (LLCs) that are treated as partnerships • Partners of limited liability partnerships (LLPs)"
findings.fix: Count a person in the helper if they have any partnership or LLC self-employment earnings (federal Schedule K-1, box 14, code A), or Schedule SE net earnings over $50,000. Simpler: ask whether you or your spouse had any self-employment or partnership earnings from business in the MCTD.

findings.who: A sole proprietor with one Schedule C showing $40,000 net profit in Queens who is also a partner with $30,000 of K-1 self-employment earnings from a Brooklyn partnership. The Zone 1 base from both sources is $70,000.
findings.why_no: The person has exactly one Schedule C and it is under $50,000. The partnership source is not counted, so the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "You must calculate your MCTMT net earnings base separately for each source of self-employment income ... If you have more than one source, combine all the individual amounts on line 54a (Zone 1 amounts) or line 54b (Zone 2 amounts)"
findings.fix: Make the helper test the combined self-employment earnings for each person across all sources (Schedule C, Schedule F, and partnership K-1), not the count or size of Schedule C forms.

findings.who: A Suffolk or Orange County farmer whose Schedule F shows $90,000 of net farm profit and who has no Schedule C.
findings.why_no: The helper looks only at Schedule C. Farm income goes on Schedule F but is still net earnings from self-employment, so the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "If an individual’s net earnings from self-employment allocated to either zone exceed $50,000 for the tax year, then you are subject to the MCTMT."
findings.fix: Base the helper on each person's Schedule SE net earnings from self-employment, which covers Schedule C, Schedule F and partnership earnings. Do not base it on Schedule C.

findings.who: A Connecticut-resident partner in a Manhattan partnership, or a consultant whose own office is in New Jersey but whose business is allocated partly to NYC.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether earnings "come from business done in New York City or the nearby counties." The filer thinks of their own work as done elsewhere and does not see that the partnership's or business's allocation percentage puts the earnings in a zone.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "To calculate your MCTMT net earnings base you must multiply your net earnings from self-employment from each source by the specific zone’s allocation percentage for each source"
findings.fix: Ask whether any business or partnership you or your spouse earned self-employment income from had business activity in the five NYC boroughs or the listed counties, wherever you live or work. Then compute or ask the allocated amount.

findings.who: A full-year New York State resident who moved into New York City on July 1, 2025, or moved out of New York City on December 31, 2025, and who has a bonus or installment-sale gain fixed in one year but reported federally in another.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about moving into New York City on January 1, 2025 or out on January 1, 2026. A mid-year or year-end move is a truthful no to both helpers.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31, Special accruals: 'Full-year and part-year New York City residents ... subject ... if you have accrued income for 2025 ... and you were a ... New York City part-year resident for tax year 2025.'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to include any New York City part-year resident for 2025, or any change of New York City residency during 2025, not only January 1 moves.

findings.who: A full-year New York State resident who lived outside New York City and moved from New Jersey to Buffalo on January 1, 2025, or from Buffalo to Florida on January 1, 2026, with income fixed in one year but reported federally in another.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about moving into or out of New York City. This filer moved into or out of New York State but not New York City, so both helpers are false.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31, Special accruals: 'Full-year New York State residents ... subject ... only if you have accrued income for 2025 and you were a nonresident of New York State on December 31, 2024; or you will be a New York State nonresident on January 1, 2026.'
findings.fix: Gate on the New York State full-year resident conditions as well as the New York City conditions: nonresident of New York State on December 31, 2024 or will be nonresident on January 1, 2026.

findings.who: On a joint return, the filer lived outside New York City all year, but the spouse moved into New York City on January 1, 2025 and has a bonus fixed in one year but reported federally in another.
findings.why_no: The gate helper says 'Moved into New York City' in the singular and does not say 'you or your spouse.' The filer truthfully answers no for himself, even though the spouse's facts trigger the special accrual rules.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31, Special accruals: 'As a full-year New York State resident for 2025, or if you are a full-year New York City resident or New York City part-year resident for 2025, you may have to use special accrual rules ...'
findings.fix: Make the gate per-person on a joint return: ask whether either spouse moved into New York City on January 1, 2025 or out on January 1, 2026, and ask the special-accrual question if either spouse meets the condition.

findings.who: A filer who had a permanent place of abode in New York City throughout 2024 and 2025, was a New York City nonresident on December 31, 2024, but met the 183-day statutory residency test for 2025 and is therefore a full-year New York City resident for 2025, with accrued income fixed in 2024 but reported federally in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether the filer 'moved into' New York City on January 1, 2025. This filer did not move; residency changed by statutory days, so the filer answers no even though the legal condition is met.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31, Special accruals: 'You are subject to the special accrual rules only if you have accrued income for 2025 ... and you were a nonresident of New York City on December 31, 2024, but you were a full-year New York City resident for tax year 2025 ...'
findings.fix: Ask the legal condition directly: were you a New York City nonresident on December 31, 2024 and a full-year New York City resident for 2025, or will you be a New York City nonresident on January 1, 2026, rather than asking only about a move.

findings.who: A filer is the designated beneficiary of a New York 529 account owned by a parent and in 2025 receives a withdrawal included in federal adjusted gross income; the filer never owns the account.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether the filer 'Owned an account in New York's 529 college savings program at any time in 2025'; a beneficiary who is not the account owner reads that as no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: 'Beneficiary During 2025, did you, as a beneficiary, receive a withdrawal ... If Yes, and you included part of the withdrawal in your federal adjusted gross income ... enter that amount on line 30.'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to cover a filer or spouse who received a New York 529 withdrawal as a beneficiary, or ask the beneficiary line 30 question outside the account-ownership gate.

findings.who: A joint return filer does not own the New York 529 account; the filer's spouse alone owns it and in 2025 makes a nonqualified withdrawal from it.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only whether 'you' owned a New York 529 account and does not say 'you or your spouse,' so the filer answers no even though the spouse's withdrawal belongs on the joint return.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 8, A-103: 'If you are filing a joint return, include the applicable amounts from all existing accounts owned by you and your spouse'; ny_it201i p. 8, Line 22 requires the Line 22 worksheet for a nonqualified withdrawal.
findings.fix: Add 'you or, on a joint return, your spouse' to the ownership gate, and keep the spouse wording in the line 22 question.

findings.who: A joint return filer does not own the New York 529 account; the filer's spouse alone owns it and in 2025 makes contributions to it, or takes a withdrawal included in federal adjusted gross income.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether 'you' owned an account and does not mention spouse; the filer answers no, although the joint return's line 30 covers the spouse's account.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: 'up to $5,000 ($10,000 for married taxpayers filing a joint return)'; ny_it225i p. 8, A-103: 'include the applicable amounts from all existing accounts owned by you and your spouse.'
findings.fix: Use an ownership gate that says 'you or your spouse' on a joint return.

findings.who: A filer owns one New York 529 account but in 2025 has no contribution to or withdrawal from it; the same filer receives a withdrawal as beneficiary of a different New York 529 account and includes part of it in federal adjusted gross income.
findings.why_no: The gated question asks only whether the filer 'put money into that New York 529 account, or take any out'; the filer truthfully says no about their own account and is not asked about the beneficiary withdrawal.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: 'Beneficiary ... If Yes, and you included part of the withdrawal in your federal adjusted gross income ... enter that amount on line 30.'
findings.fix: Add 'or receive a withdrawal as a beneficiary included in federal adjusted gross income' to the line 30 question, or ask a separate beneficiary question.

findings.who: A filer, or a spouse on a joint return, born between January 1 and July 1, 1966, who received a taxable IRA, 401(k) or private pension distribution in the second half of 2025, after turning 59½ during the year.
findings.why_no: The gate counts only recipients born in 1965 or earlier. Its helper text claims that this means '59½ or older at some time in 2025', but a person born in the first half of 1966 reaches 59½ between July and December 2025. The computed count is therefore 0, and that person is never asked.
findings.line: ny_it201.pension_exclusion_if_young (and the line 29 exclusion or refusal it leads to)
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: 'If you became 59½ during 2025, enter only the amount you received after you became 59½, but not more than $20,000.'
findings.fix: Count recipients born before July 2, 1966, not 'in 1965 or earlier'. Better, ask the line 29 question whenever any taxable pension, annuity or IRA income exists, and let the filer give the date they turned 59½.

findings.who: A filer under 59½ (born after mid-1966) who received taxable distributions as the beneficiary of a deceased parent's IRA or pension, where the decedent would have qualified for the exclusion.
findings.why_no: The gate checks only the recipient's own birth year, so no recipient is counted. The beneficiary clause exists only inside the gated question, and that question is reached only through this gate. In addition, the line's 'Otherwise: false, and the question below is not asked' means that when the gate is false the question is never asked at all. The beneficiary branch is unreachable.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: 'If you received pension and annuity income and are married, or received pension and annuity income as a beneficiary, see Married taxpayers or Beneficiaries below.'
findings.fix: Make the gate 'any person had taxable pension, annuity or IRA income' (count > 0), with no age filter. Then ask whether the recipient turned 59½ by December 31, 2025, or received the money as the beneficiary of someone who died.

findings.who: Any filer whose gate evaluates false, that is, every young or beneficiary recipient of private pension or IRA income.
findings.why_no: The line's logic is self-defeating. When the gate holds, the choice resolves to 'No' because a recipient was born in 1965 or earlier. When the gate fails, the line is forced to false and the question is not asked. No path ever asks the question or yields yes.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: 'Did you enter an amount of pension income or annuity income, or both ... that was not from a New York State or local government pension plan or federal government pension plan?'
findings.fix: Invert the gate so the question is asked when no recipient is known to be 59½. Alternatively, drop the gate and ask whenever taxable pension, annuity or IRA income exists, since the tool must refuse or compute in either case.

findings.who: A filer 59½ or older whose only qualifying income is periodic distributions from a government 457 plan, a 403(b) or a 401(k), which they do not think of as 'pension or IRA money'.
findings.why_no: The question says 'that pension or IRA money', and the help mentions only 'such income'. A filer with a 401(k) or 457 plan may read this as excluding their plan.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: qualifying income includes 'periodic distributions from government (IRC § 457) deferred compensation plans' and 'a qualified cash or deferred profit-sharing or stock bonus plan [IRC § 401(k)]'.
findings.fix: Name the plan types in the question: 'pension, annuity, IRA, 401(k), 403(b), Keogh, or government 457 plan distributions'.

findings.who: Married filing jointly; the filer is a private-sector employee and the spouse is a New York City public school teacher in the NYC Teachers' Retirement System whose W-2 shows 414(h) contributions.
findings.why_no: The gate is cited as 'Are you a public employee...' and does not say 'you or your spouse'; the filer answers no about themself, though the joint return includes the spouse's W-2.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 21: 'If Yes, enter the amount of 414(h) retirement contributions, if shown on any federal Form W-2' and includes the New York City Teachers' Retirement System.
findings.fix: Ask 'Are you or your spouse a public employee...' or compute the gate from any W-2 on the joint return.

findings.who: A filer who was a New York State employee until retiring or leaving in June 2025 and now works in the private sector; the 2025 state W-2 shows a 414(h) contribution.
findings.why_no: The question uses the present tense 'Are you a public employee'; at filing time they are not, so they answer no even though they had a New York public employer during 2025.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 21: 'If Yes, enter the amount of 414(h) retirement contributions, if shown on any federal Form W-2' for a member of the listed New York retirement systems.
findings.fix: Ask 'Were you (or your spouse) a public employee at any time during 2025...' or use any 2025 W-2.

findings.who: An employee of MABSTOA (or another New York public authority/public benefit corporation) who participates in the MABSTOA Pension Plan and has 414(h) contributions shown on a W-2; they are not employed by the state or a local government.
findings.why_no: They read 'public employee of New York State or its local governments' as excluding a public authority or public benefit corporation, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 21: 'a member of the Manhattan and Bronx Surface Transit Operating Authority (MABSTOA) Pension Plan.'
findings.fix: Ask 'public employee of New York State, a local government, or a New York public authority/public benefit corporation' or use the retirement-system list in the instructions.

findings.who: A public employee whose W-2 box 14 shows a pension pickup under a label such as 'NYSLRS' or 'PENSION' rather than the literal '414(h)'.
findings.why_no: The gated question asks whether the W-2 shows a '414(h) retirement contribution (usually in box 14)'; not seeing that exact label, they answer no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 21: 'enter the amount of 414(h) retirement contributions, if shown on any federal Form W-2' (it does not require the W-2 label to say '414(h)').
findings.fix: Ask whether box 14 shows any retirement/pension pickup for a listed New York public retirement system, and give examples of common box 14 labels.
